title: NHS restructuring: savings, services and local relationships
label: 16 November 2026 · NHS restructuring
summary: The Committee examined the reorganisation of Integrated Care Boards (ICBs), which plan and fund NHS services locally, including the aim of cutting their running costs by 43% and reducing their workforce. NHS England said the changes should remove duplicated work, clarify responsibilities and help ICBs focus on choosing services that best meet local needs. Members challenged whether savings and promised improvements can be demonstrated without losing important skills, weakening patient services or damaging relationships with councils and general practice. Officials said most restructuring was complete and remained under review, but acknowledged disruption and promised further information on costs, staffing and ICB plans. The Committee remained concerned that the financial and service effects, and the future shape of local partnerships, were not yet clear.

glossary.definition: Integrated Care Boards: local NHS organisations that plan and pay for health services for their populations.
The national body that oversees and supports the NHS in England.
Deciding which services and support to fund, based on what will most improve health for local people.
A temporary NHS organisation set up to carry out particular functions.
Groups of organisations that deliver NHS care and work together to plan or improve services.
Support for children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities.
The measures and checks used by NHS England to monitor how local NHS organisations are performing.

chapters.title: Why restructure, and what should it achieve?
chapters.takeaway: Officials argued that reducing duplicated management should free money and attention for patient care, but members wanted evidence of lasting benefits.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: ICBs plan and fund NHS services for local populations. They were responsible for £171 billion of NHS spending in 2025-26. NHS England wants them to cut running costs by 43%, saving £908 million a year, which is expected to mean about 8,000 fewer posts.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The question is whether these changes will improve care, not simply cut administration. Can you update us on the estimated cost of the wider reorganisation?

turns.speaker: Samantha Jones
turns.text: The estimated cost of reducing staff at the centre is about £1 billion to £1.3 billion, depending partly on individual circumstances. We remain on track to make £1 billion of savings over this Parliament.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: What will local people gain from the ICB changes? There is concern that this is mainly about cutting jobs and costs.

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: The financial pressure was real, but it wasn't the only reason. Responsibilities had become confusing, with several levels sometimes overseeing the same work. Providers told us the system was complicated and unbalanced.

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: We wanted clearer decisions and a system that could improve services faster. ICB leaders now tell us the painful changes have helped them focus on choosing where money will do the most good. They say they're beginning to see improvements, though we still need to test that.

turns.speaker: Jan Thomas
turns.text: The aim of strategic commissioning is to ask, 'If we have limited money, where should we spend it next to improve health?' That means looking at people's needs and preventing illness from getting worse, not just funding a service because someone can show it works.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: That sounds like work ICBs should always have been doing. What is genuinely different now?

turns.speaker: Jan Thomas
turns.text: We hadn't been doing it well enough. ICBs are now working together on five measures, including emergency visits, outpatient referrals and access to same-day urgent care. The idea is to learn and act together, rather than relying on scattered local efforts.

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: We also wanted ICBs to focus on commissioning rather than trying to manage every provider's performance themselves. Other parts of the NHS already did some of that work.

chapters.title: Job cuts, skills and the cost of change
chapters.takeaway: Officials said the cuts were aimed at management and duplicated tasks, but the Committee demanded clarity about lost skills, redundancy costs and whether patient services were affected.

turns.speaker: Al Carns
turns.text: About 3,000 ICB staff had left through redundancy by June. Are you tracking which grades and skills are going, and checking that the cuts aren't producing harmful gaps?

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: We have asked ICB leaders whether their new organisations have the skills to do the job, rather than just whether they have met a headcount target. Some have identified gaps or said staff need to be moved between teams. This is still work in progress.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth O’Mahony
turns.text: By August, about 8,000 people had left: around 4,200 through voluntary redundancy, 230 through compulsory redundancy, and about 3,000 through other routes such as taking another job or leaving a vacancy unfilled. ICB boards have reviewed staffing and whether important skills are being kept.

turns.speaker: Mr Betts
turns.text: It sounds hard to tell patients that cutting thousands of staff will improve their care. Were these people doing work that mattered?

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: We targeted work away from staff providing direct care. Those affected were often doing support work, but that doesn't mean it had no value.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth O’Mahony
turns.text: Some work, especially monitoring provider performance, was being repeated at ICB, regional and national levels. The amount spent on ICB administration varied widely, without a clear link to better patient outcomes.

turns.speaker: Jan Thomas
turns.text: Some hands-on responsibilities, such as safeguarding, medicines support and care for people with complex needs, have been protected. For service redesign, we want clinicians and the organisations running services to lead more of the work, rather than having ICB teams try to organise it for them.

turns.speaker: Mr Betts
turns.text: But are providers taking on extra work, or were they doing it already?

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: Mostly they were already involved, sometimes through joint working groups. We believe the people delivering care are better placed to change how care is organised. We are trying to remove duplication, not simply shift work without a plan.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The report says £582 million was recorded for redundancy costs up to March. If that figure rose in line with the number of people leaving, it could exceed the expected savings. Please send us a clear breakdown that reconciles the dates, costs and projected savings, including what happens if someone takes another NHS job soon after leaving.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth O’Mahony
turns.text: That figure includes estimates for people who hadn't yet left, including pension costs, and the figures cover different periods. A table will help explain how they fit together.

chapters.title: Measuring progress and protecting statutory services
chapters.takeaway: NHS England said ICBs report against performance and cost measures, but members questioned whether those checks will reveal harm early enough.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: A collection of success stories isn't enough. How will you measure whether the reorganisation improves services as a whole?

turns.speaker: Jan Thomas
turns.text: We're refining a national set of 38 measures, covering areas such as health inequalities and use of services. ICBs are also working together on five measures, including emergency visits, outpatient referrals, hospital stays for people over 65, children's dentistry and same-day urgent care.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: Those sound like targets for managing services, rather than measures of better health or reduced inequality.

turns.speaker: Jan Thomas
turns.text: We use them as warning signs. If people keep needing emergency care, it may show that support in the community isn't working well enough. The aim is to spot that and improve the whole system, not just spend more on one service.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: The report says some ICBs thought the changes would make it harder to meet duties such as safeguarding, care assessments and support for children with additional needs. What assurance can you give patients?

turns.speaker: Jan Thomas
turns.text: During the restructure there was disruption, including staff leaving and teams being rebuilt. ICBs have since worked to put people in the right roles, particularly for safeguarding and care for people with the greatest needs. Their boards remain responsible for meeting those duties.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: How will you check for delays in these services, such as decisions about care or education support?

turns.speaker: Jan Thomas
turns.text: Each ICB board monitors its services, including how quickly continuing-care decisions are made. Regional colleagues challenge an ICB if its results worsen, and ask what it will do to improve.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: Will you repeat the survey of ICBs' concerns in six months and share the results?

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: We'll use a wider review of the changes rather than create several separate exercises. The process was rushed and at times chaotic: we didn't have all the approvals, funding arrangements and communications ready in advance. Staff faced a lot of uncertainty.

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: The situation has improved in recent months, but we should not pretend the change was painless. We will review whether the new arrangements work and keep watching for problems.

chapters.title: Are the savings and new structures secure?
chapters.takeaway: Officials said most ICBs had confirmed their plans and were close to their cost targets, while acknowledging that the Committee had not received all the evidence it sought.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: There are now 25 ICBs, but the report describes slow progress and incomplete information. Have all of them confirmed the structures they plan to use?

turns.speaker: Jan Thomas
turns.text: Each has gone through a review with regional NHS colleagues, who checked whether it could carry out its responsibilities. We have details of their plans.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: Have you received future projections of redundancies from each one?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth O’Mahony
turns.text: We don't collect those projections. ICBs tell us whether they expect to stay within their running-cost budgets and meet their responsibilities. Across the programme, 7,753 people had left against an overall target of about 8,000, and we don't expect a large new round of redundancies.

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: If an ICB planned a major further change involving hundreds of job losses, we would expect its leaders to tell us through the regional system. We would work with them on it.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: One ICB was late to complete its changes, and another is still aiming to meet its running-cost target by year-end. Do all ICBs now assure you they can do the job effectively?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth O’Mahony
turns.text: The late case was a London ICB that joined a group later than others. It says it will meet its costs by year-end. We'll check progress again during the year and step in if it looks likely to miss.

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: We believe the ICBs can meet their budgets and responsibilities. Their total running costs had grown from about £1 billion to £2.2 billion within a few years, which we considered unsustainable. Boards must now show they can spend within their reduced budgets.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How will you stop staff numbers and costs creeping back up, and ensure ICBs haven't lost critical skills?

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: We will review budgets, plans and results regularly, and check whether boards can still carry out their duties. But local boards are responsible for keeping the right skills and using money wisely; national checks can't replace that responsibility.

turns.speaker: Tristan Osborne
turns.text: Please send us a table showing each ICB's plan, its confidence in meeting the cost target, and whether its structure is in place.

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: We can provide that, along with the information the Chair requested on redundancy costs and savings.

chapters.title: Working with councils, clinicians and local areas
chapters.takeaway: Officials said partnership work should continue through local teams and care providers, but members raised concerns that fewer named contacts could weaken established relationships.

turns.speaker: Mr Betts
turns.text: Local authorities and the NHS have a long history of planning services together. Are councils concerned that cuts have left them with nobody in ICBs to work with?

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: Some places have lost small teams that worked closely with councils, and people are still adjusting to new contacts. There are still staff responsible for working with councils, but the arrangements are different.

turns.speaker: Jan Thomas
turns.text: Some work is now done across a larger area to save money, but local teams still need to plan with each council. In my area, for example, we worked on separate plans with each of seven local authorities, rather than imposing one plan on all of them.

turns.speaker: Mr Betts
turns.text: Have social care and public health leaders told you that the NHS is pushing work onto them?

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: I haven't received complaints saying that services have been disabled. Council leaders initially had concerns because a key partner was changing, but in our latest discussion they said things were starting to settle.

turns.speaker: Mr Betts
turns.text: We have heard that local authorities are struggling to get enough ICB staff involved in safeguarding.

turns.speaker: Jan Thomas
turns.text: ICBs have a legal duty to work with councils and police on safeguarding. The change meant people had to rebuild working relationships, but boards still have to make sure the duty is met.

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: No specific safeguarding problem has been raised with us recently. These arrangements involve several agencies, so if they weren't working, we would expect to hear about it quickly.

turns.speaker: Mr Betts
turns.text: The Royal College of GPs says clinical leadership has been lost. Have ICBs lost the direct input of GPs and other clinicians?

turns.speaker: Jan Thomas
turns.text: ICBs aren't organised like the earlier GP-led groups, but clinical advice is still part of their work. They also draw on doctors, nurses, GPs, pharmacists and other clinicians through care providers, local networks and joint working groups.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: General practices have also reported problems with their IT support, delayed payments and not knowing who to contact.

turns.speaker: Jan Thomas
turns.text: Experiences vary, and I would like details so we can follow up. Support for GP computer systems has been particularly difficult during the changes to other NHS support organisations. That's different from the way ICBs work with GPs on everyday services.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: If joint working happens outside ICBs, how will you make sure hospitals don't dominate and that primary and community care have a strong voice?

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: That's a real risk. Better links between general practice and hospitals are essential, and leaders must treat working with councils and primary care as part of their job. We need to share examples of what works and involve primary-care leaders.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: People have built up knowledge and relationships across health services, councils and community groups. How do you preserve that if the staff who held those relationships leave?

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: Those relationships shouldn't have to run through the ICB's formal structure. Clinicians, councils and services can work through local teams, neighbourhood arrangements or groups of care providers. But we need to make sure those links continue in practice.

chapters.title: National changes, devolution and next steps
chapters.takeaway: The future division of responsibilities remains unsettled as NHS England is absorbed into the Department and local boundaries are reorganised.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: NHS England is due to be abolished and most of its staff and functions transferred to the Department of Health and Social Care. How will you address differences in pay for people doing similar work?

turns.speaker: Samantha Jones
turns.text: The Secretary of State has proposed a temporary NHS body for regional functions, so staff who support local NHS delivery remain within the health service. Pay arrangements for people moving between organisations are still being discussed with unions.

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: There will be a process to bring pay arrangements closer together, agreed with unions. Comparing salary figures alone can be misleading because pensions and other terms also differ.

turns.speaker: Rachel Gilmour
turns.text: How do we know this temporary body won't simply add another layer of bureaucracy?

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: It is meant to be temporary and to keep regional staff focused on supporting local NHS services while we work out how health services fit with devolution. We decided against making regions separate permanent organisations because that could add complexity.

turns.speaker: Mr Betts
turns.text: How long will the temporary body last? Could its staff eventually move into mayoral authorities?

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: We can't give a fixed end date. It will need to last long enough to align responsibilities with local government and mayoral areas, which could take years. Some work might move to local authorities, ICBs or providers, depending on what works best.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: The Government wants ICB boundaries to match mayoral areas by 2028. Is that achievable alongside local-government reform?

turns.speaker: Samantha Jones
turns.text: That is the timetable set by the Prime Minister and Secretary of State. We need to understand the final boundaries and how the arrangements will work.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: My area was merged before we knew which mayoral area it might join. Could that mean another reorganisation?

turns.speaker: Jan Thomas
turns.text: Possibly, but we have paused some full legal mergers while boundaries are uncertain. ICBs can work as a group under one leadership team without closing the existing legal organisations. That gives us more room to adjust later.

turns.speaker: Samantha Jones
turns.text: There is a risk that some boundaries will need to change. We are trying to limit further disruption while still making services as local as possible.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Will rural ICBs receive extra support because delivering healthcare over long distances costs more?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth O’Mahony
turns.text: The £19.60 per person target is for ICB running costs, not the cost of delivering healthcare. The money for care is allocated separately, using a formula that takes account of factors including rurality, age and deprivation.

turns.speaker: Mr Betts
turns.text: Knowing how difficult the process was, would you still have reorganised the NHS in this way?

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: Yes. I believed responsibilities had become confusing, duplicated and too expensive. But we should have communicated better and had approvals and redundancy arrangements ready before the changes began. The uncertainty was extremely difficult for staff.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: What worries you most now, and has the reorganisation distracted staff from preparing for winter?

turns.speaker: Sir Jim Mackey
turns.text: The NHS still isn't meeting the standards patients deserve; having people treated in corridors is unacceptable. Change has been a distraction, but I don't think it explains the current pressure on urgent care. Demand has risen, and there have also been difficult weather and infrastructure problems.

turns.speaker: Samantha Jones
turns.text: Winter support depends on the NHS, social care and local government working together. Their work through the reorganisation and through winter is a joint effort.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We still need clear evidence about the savings, redundancy costs, local partnerships and the services that will be delivered. We expect the promised notes and will consider the evidence before making recommendations.
